children: remains close to record highs, but BTIG technical strategist Jonathan Krinsky says a growing number of market internals are starting to “rhyme with 2000.”
Krinsky said the most obvious warning sign is the widening dispersion beneath the major indexes.
is roughly 14% below its June high, but the average stock in the index is down about 26% from its 52-week high, while 10 of the 30 constituents remain more than 30% below their peaks.

BTIG said that kind of divergence has precedent. After the SOX peaked in March 2000, 13 of the 20 current constituents that were members of the index at the time went on to make fresh 52-week highs even though the broader semiconductor index had already peaked. Krinsky said that suggests individual stocks can continue to rally after the broader group has made its final high.

The same narrowing is showing up across the S&P 500. The index has gained 1.2% over the past month even though 9 of 11 sectors are negative, and it has posted five-straight sessions with more stocks making 52-week lows than highs despite trading near all-time highs.
Banks are another concern. The KBW Bank Index
is more than 10% below its 30-day high while the S&P 500 remains within 1% of a 52-week high. BTIG said the last time that combination occurred was January 2000.
Krinsky is not calling for an immediate breakdown. The Nasdaq 100

remains technically strong, and BTIG sees a near-term breakout as likely. But fewer than 60% of Nasdaq 100 stocks are above their 200-day moving averages, while a historical study of the current setup points to stronger five-day returns that turn negative in the 30-40 day window.

“Adding it all up,” Krinsky said it remains difficult to fight tech momentum in the near term, but the extreme dispersion and growing number of 2000-style signals keep BTIG cautious over the medium term.
